transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Jared Li (Redwood SE), Priya Sinha (Redwood SE), Maya Ramesh (Tidewave ML), Sam Ortiz (Tidewave Platform), Lena Koh (Tidewave PM)

Auto-summary: KV hit-rate dropped from ~62% to ~34% after prod traffic change; suspicion is prefix variation + TTL churn; proposed experiments around eviction (LFU), aggressive prefix canonicalization, and warmed prefetch sizing.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, we wanted to get back together on the cache triage, quick check — is this still the same 2x traffic burst pattern you saw last week?
[00:00:14] Maya: Yeah for sure, we pushed the new search pipeline on Wed so the distribution changed, we see more long tails in prompts and, um, a lot of slightly different prefixes.
[00:00:22] Sam: And latency's fine generally but cost spiked because of token churn, so the cache hit rate drop is... noticeable.
[00:00:28] Jared: Okay, quick confirmation — before the deploy you were at ~62% KV hit, after deploy around 34%? can you confirm the exact numbers?
[00:00:36] Maya: Correct, it's 61.8 down to 33.9 over the 48 hour window. There's a blip at 02:00 when the batch job ran but it's mostly steady.
[00:00:44] Priya: Two obvious culprits: more unique prefixes (prefix variance) and higher churn of TTL'd entries because of shorter-lived sessions.
[00:00:51] Lena: We also changed some of the per-request metadata — added a 'region' key in the prompt envelope, maybe that is breaking prefix equivalence.
[00:01:00] Alex: Good, that's helpful. Couple notes: Redwood's KV cache keying is agnostic but if you add ephemeral fields into the prefix, that definitely fragments keys.
[00:01:09] Speaker 1: (inaudible but talking about) oh right yeah
[00:01:14] Jared: We pulled a sample of the top 10k prefixes yesterday — many of them differ by small tokens at the end or by JSON-ish metadata. We'll attach that sample.
[00:01:23] Sam: When you say 'attach' is that in the shared drive? we can't share PII but we can anonymize.
[00:01:29] Alex: Totally. Give us anonymized shapes, hashed keys, counts — that's enough.
[00:01:33] Maya: We can send the top-50 by freq, hashed and with their counts, that'll be quick.
[00:01:37] Jared: Great. On the eviction side, what are you currently running — LRU?
[00:01:41] Sam: Yeah, default LRU with a soft TTL of 24h, hard TTL of 72h.
[00:01:46] Priya: LRU doesn't always handle heavy long-tail skew well, esp when you have lots of near-unique prefixes — LFU or a tiny hybrid can help.
[00:01:54] Alex: We suggested LFU in the doc last week as an experiment. Jared, are you able to run a synthetic benchmark to measure LFU vs LRU under their workload?
[00:02:03] Jared: Yes I can. Plan would be to replay a 2x QPS trace for 3 hours, enable metrics for hit-rate, eviction churn, cold-start latency. I'll push the run and share graphs.
[00:02:12] Lena: For the replay, what's the minimal dataset you need?
[00:02:16] Jared: Top-50k hashed keys and relative frequency distribution would be perfect, but top-5k could still show the delta.
[00:02:22] Maya: We'll export a 48h sample and trim to top-10k hashed prefixes, ok.
[00:02:26] Alex: Another quick win is prefix normalization. We saw in the sample a bunch of trailing timestamps and region tags — if you canonicalize before keying, you regain a lot of hit-rate.
[00:02:36] Sam: On our side that's doable; it's a small transform in the service layer, but we worry about getting mutants where we accidentally normalize out important signal.
[00:02:44] Priya: Totally — make the normalization conservative and pilot in pre-prod. Our normalization script can be a drop-in: strip known metadata keys, collapse whitespace, canonicalize iso-dates to day buckets, etc.
[00:02:55] Maya: Can you share that script?
[00:02:58] Alex: Yes, I'll push a small script and README. We'll include toggles so you can turn on rules one by one.
[00:03:03] Speaker 2: [crosstalk]
[00:03:10] Jared: On metrics, please also enable per-prefix TTL distribution and per-prefix request counts — this will help differentiate high-frequency short-lived vs low-frequency long-lived keys.
[00:03:18] Sam: We can add that, but it will increase metrics cardinality — will that blow up your dashboards?
[00:03:24] Priya: We recommend sampling for low-freq prefixes and full coverage for top-n to keep cardinality controlled.
[00:03:31] Lena: About warmup/prefetch — we were trying a prefetch of top-500 at service start, but when burst came it still didn't help. Any ideas?
[00:03:40] Alex: Prefetch helps if your top items are stable; if the top-500 changes with traffic shift it's wasted. Consider a lightweight warm-up that rehydrates the top-1% of traffic in the last hour, and pair with a short-lived LFU so the warmed keys stick.
[00:03:53] Maya: Hmm ok, so warmup + LFU to keep warmed entries. That sounds promising.
[00:03:58] Jared: We'll test warmup variants in the synthetic run: baseline (none), static top-500, dynamic top-1% rolling.
[00:04:06] Alex: Also think about short TTL bump for warmed keys — e.g., if warmed keys get a reserved TTL or not counted in eviction immediately. We have a warm-bit technique in our notes.
[00:04:15] Sam: Would that require code change to tag keys?
[00:04:18] Priya: Minimal — at write time add a small attribute, Redwood runtime can honor warm-bit for eviction heuristics.
[00:04:24] Maya: Ok, tech debt question: how intrusive is enabling LFU in your environment?
[00:04:29] Jared: It's a config flip at the runtime layer, but we need to validate performance under load. LFU has heavier bookkeeping so there might be a small CPU overhead. We'll measure it in the synthetic run.
[00:04:38] Lena: If LFU costs us CPU and increases latency slightly, we need to quantify cost vs hit-rate benefit.
[00:04:43] Alex: Exactly, that's why the benchmark will include cost proxies — tokens served, throughput, per-request p50/p95 latency, and CPU usage.
[00:04:50] Speaker 3: [pause]
[00:04:55] Maya: Another oddity — some prefixes that used to be high-frequency became mid-frequency, likely due to a different front-end flow. Could that cause fragmentation with near-duplicates?
[00:05:03] Alex: Yes, any change in client shaping can move topography. That's why combining normalization + eviction experiment is important. Try normalization first in pre-prod, then LFU in canary.
[00:05:14] Sam: On the prompt reuse side, how are we measuring reuse? We installed the telemetry but not sure the schema is right.
[00:05:20] Jared: Current telemetry tracks hashed input prefix and counts, but we missed tagging when a prompt is rewritten by the front-end (e.g., micro-templates). We need to track canonical templates too.
[00:05:30] Priya: Suggest adding a template-id at the application layer so you can fold variants together into the same reuse bucket. Minimal instrument change.
[00:05:36] Maya: I'll check with front-end on feasibility.
[00:05:40] Lena: For the normalization script, can you include a dry-run mode that maps before->after so we can inspect the impact?
[00:05:46] Alex: Yep, that's standard. Dry-run with counts and a threshold. Also include a revert.
[00:05:52] Speaker 1: (mutter) makes sense
[00:05:58] Alex: Ok timing — Jared will run the synthetic tonight or tomorrow and share results; Maya will send logs; I will push script. Then we'll reconvene mid-next-week to pick eviction policy.
[00:06:09] Maya: Quick question — any security concerns with sending hashed prefixes?
[00:06:14] Alex: Hashing + removal of PII fields is fine; we'll sign an NDA if required, but hashed shapes are usually acceptable.
[00:06:21] Sam: We'll produce a scrubbed sample then.
[00:06:24] Jared: One technical note — when comparing LFU vs LRU please also look at cold-start penalties for KV misses; sometimes LFU keeps hot-but-infrequent items and LRU evicts those differently.
[00:06:34] Priya: Also track reclaim churn — number of evictions per minute — that tells you thrashing.
[00:06:39] Alex: Good. Anything else on metrics?
[00:06:42] Lena: Could you add a small dashboard template we can import?
[00:06:45] Jared: We'll export a dashboard with hit-rate, evictions/min, CPU, p50/p95, warmed-key-count.
[00:06:53] Maya: Thanks. A process question — if the LFU experiment shows marginal uplift but bigger CPU cost, do we have hybrid options?
[00:06:59] Alex: Yes, hybrid heuristics exist: segmented LFU where you keep LRU for a lower tier and LFU for the top tier, or sample-based LFU to reduce overhead. We'll outline options in the write-up.
[00:07:11] Sam: Good. On rollout risk — what's the rollback plan if we see regression?
[00:07:16] Priya: Canary with traffic split and automatic fallback to LRU if hit-rate goes below threshold or latency grows. Redwood runtime supports policy-based fallback.
[00:07:24] Maya: Perfect.
[00:07:28] Alex: Let's capture action items and dates (we'll add to the CRM).
[00:07:33] Speaker 2: [brief silence]
[00:07:38] Alex: Any blockers from your side?
[00:07:41] Maya: None, aside from getting the logs out.
[00:07:44] Sam: We'll get them scraped and delivered by tomorrow morning.
[00:07:48] Lena: Ok, thanks all.
[00:07:50] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up in a thread with the script and benchmark plan.

(End of meeting - remaining ~39 minutes were used for a quick screenshare and looking at the sample prefixes; transcript clipped per meeting policy)
